title: Haredi Judaism
hook: "those who tremble": close-knit communities devoted to Torah study

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: binding tradition. Orthodox Judaism holds the Torah as given by God and halakha as binding, and it has several streams inside it. Did you take the pause before a bite? Today, the first stream. Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

Close to midnight, and the room is still full: tables, open books, and noise. Two people lean over one page of Talmud, and one of them is jabbing the margin with a finger. Across the table, another pair is arguing about the same line from the other side. Nobody is shushing anybody. This is a study hall, a beit midrash, and in the communities we meet today, a room like this sits near the center of life. From outside, people tend to notice the dark coats and hats. From inside, people tend to talk about the page. Today's word.
screen: `A LOUD ROOM OF BOOKS.` → `TWO PEOPLE, ONE PAGE.` → `THE PAGE AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Haredi. Turn it four ways. First, the name comes from a verse. Isaiah says: "Hear the word of the LORD, ye that tremble at his word." In Hebrew, those who tremble is haredim. So the name is not about fear of people. It describes awe before the word of God, a seriousness about it that shapes a whole life. Second, study. God tells Joshua the book of the law should not leave his mouth: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." Haredi communities take that line close to literally. Boys and young men may spend long years in a yeshiva, and some married men keep learning in a kollel, a study hall for adults, while the family's life is arranged to support it. Women learn too, in their own schools, and in some families carry much of the work outside the home. Third, community. Haredi life is close-knit on purpose: its own schools, its own neighborhoods, a careful distance from much of the wider culture's media. Inside, there are free-loan funds, meals brought to new mothers, and help for anyone in trouble. And Haredi Judaism is not one thing. Some communities are Hasidic, gathered around a rebbe. Others center on the yeshivas and their heads. There are Sephardi Haredi communities too. Fourth, why study holds that place. The Mishnah lists good deeds whose fruit a person enjoys in this world, honoring parents, acts of kindness, making peace between people, and ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all. Elsewhere the Talmud's sages ask which is greater, study or doing, and answer: study, because study leads to doing. In this view, the open book is where every other good thing begins.
screen: `YE THAT TREMBLE AT HIS WORD.` · `DAY AND NIGHT: A LIFE OF STUDY.` · `CLOSE-KNIT ON PURPOSE.` · `STUDY LEADS TO DOING.` · then, large: `DEVOTED STUDY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect one devoted way of life. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose life is shaped by a devotion you don't share. A religious neighbor, a monk, an athlete in training, a grandparent who never missed a morning prayer. Leave aside whether you'd live that way. Just look at what it costs them, and what it gives them. See their ordinary day from the inside for a moment, the early alarm, the choices, the joy in it. If you pray, you can hold them in that prayer. Then let the picture rest. The bell holds the time.
Haredi. Those who tremble at God's word, from Isaiah: close-knit communities, Hasidic and others, that put the study of Torah at the center of life. Today's word.
Your line: devoted study. Today, give one page of something that matters to you your full attention, the way two learners lean over one line. Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Haredi Jews keep halakha in full and build close-knit communities around Torah study, with yeshivas for young men, kollels for married men, schools for girls and women, and strong networks of mutual help.

notes: Isaiah 66:5's Hebrew is ha-haredim el devaro; the lesson says the name comes from this verse (the outline gives 'those who tremble'). Some trace the usage also to Isaiah 66:2; confirm.
Descriptions of Haredi community life (free-loan funds, meal help, distance from wider media, women's schooling and work) are general and unsourced; please check they are fair and not stereotyping.

Mishnah Peah 1:1 and Kiddushin 40b ('study is greater, for it leads to action') are paraphrased; the Mishnah's full list also includes early arrival at the study house and other items in the version recited in the morning service.
Litvish/'yeshivish' communities are described only as 'centered on the great yeshivas'.
